usage: Said to others, never about your own plate
examples: 맛있게 드세요.
Enjoy your meal.
The bare minimum a server says while setting down a plate — short, warm, sufficient on its own.
A: 이거 제가 직접 만들었어요. / B: 와, 진짜요? 맛있게 먹을게요!
A: I made this myself. / B: Really? I'll enjoy it!
A/B exchange: the guest responds with 먹을게요 (casual self-announcement) rather than repeating 드세요 back, since you do not wish yourself a good meal with 드세요.
주문하신 음식 다 나왔습니다. 맛있게 드세요.
All your dishes have come out. Please enjoy.
Real restaurant line; 나왔습니다 marks the food's arrival — the full 합쇼체 form signals professional service register.
nuance: 맛있게 드세요 literally stacks 맛있게 'deliciously' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 들다/먹다 'to eat', so it means 'please eat (this) deliciously' — a warm wish aimed at the other person, never a comment on your own food. The adverb 맛있게 is what distinguishes it from plain 드세요 ('please eat'): removing it strips the warmth entirely and leaves a bare instruction. Honorific 드세요 is required for guests, elders, and customers; the casual equivalent for close friends or children is 맛있게 먹어. Common collocates: 많이 드세요 (eat a lot), 천천히 드세요 (no rush), 따뜻할 때 드세요 (while it's warm). English speakers most often make the register error of dropping the honorific (먹으세요) or, worse, saying 맛있게 드세요 before their own meal — but the phrase cannot be aimed at yourself; say 잘 먹겠습니다 instead when you are the one sitting down to eat.

structuredNuance.t: Word for word: 맛있게 = 'deliciously' + 드세요 = honorific imperative of '먹다 to eat'. Real meaning: 'please eat this and find it delicious' — a warm wish about taste and enjoyment, not just an order to eat.

Service staff → customer, host → guest, parent → elder relative: all use 드세요. To a close friend or a child you can soften to 맛있게 먹어. Never say it about your own meal — for that, 잘 먹겠습니다 before eating, 잘 먹었습니다 after.

드세요 alone = plain 'please eat' with no warmth. 맛있게 드세요 adds the taste-wish. 잘 드세요 ('eat well') exists but is less common in this fixed send-off role. 천천히 드세요 focuses on pace rather than taste — it can follow 맛있게 드세요 for a layered farewell.
Casual: 맛있게 먹어 (반말). More formal: 맛있게 드십시오 (합쇼체, announcements). Layered: 맛있게 드시고 천천히 드세요. Past: 맛있게 드셨어요? (checking afterward).

English speakers say 맛있게 드세요 before their own meal, mapping it onto 'bon appétit'. But you cannot wish yourself a good meal with 드세요 — the honorific imperative points outward. Before your own meal: 잘 먹겠습니다. Also, never swap 드세요 for 먹으세요 with elders — 먹다 lacks the honorific register.

mistakes: Saying 맛있게 드세요 about your own meal before you eat.
The phrase is a wish directed at others; you cannot tell yourself to enjoy. Say 잘 먹겠습니다 ('I will eat well') to your host instead.
Using 먹으세요 to a guest or elder.
먹다 is the plain verb; to someone you respect the honorific 들다 is expected, so 드세요, not 먹으세요, sounds properly polite.
Treating 맛있게 as optional filler and dropping it.
Bare 드세요 just means 'eat'; the warmth and the 'enjoy' meaning live entirely in 맛있게, so omitting it changes the tone.

english: I look forward to working with you
usage: Please take good care of it / me
I look forward to working with you
Please treat me well going forward
examples: 잘 부탁드려요.
I look forward to working with you.
Standalone closer at first introductions — no extra context needed; the social bow does the work.
A: 오늘부터 우리 팀에 합류하게 됐어요. / B: 반갑습니다, 잘 부탁드려요!
A: I've joined your team starting today. / B: Nice to meet you, I look forward to working with you!
Natural office exchange: A announces, B returns the same formula, establishing mutual goodwill at once.
우리 아이 잘 부탁드리겠습니다.
Please take good care of my child.
Parent to teacher at a school; 드리겠습니다 is the humblest form, showing the speaker is entrusting something precious.
nuance: 부탁 is Sino-Korean 付託 'to entrust/commit a request', and 드리다 is the humble 'give (upward to a superior)', so 부탁드려요 literally means 'I humbly hand you my request'. Add 잘 ('well/kindly') and it becomes the all-purpose Korean phrase for 'please look after me/this kindly'. It has no single English equivalent — context shifts it between 'nice to meet you', 'I look forward to working with you', and 'please take care of it'. The nearest comparison is 도와주세요 ('please help me'), which is a concrete ask for a specific action; 잘 부탁드려요 is softer social glue asking for general goodwill, not any particular task. Scale of formality: casual 부탁해 (반말, friends only) → 부탁해요 → 부탁드려요 → 부탁드립니다 → 부탁드리겠습니다. English speakers most often misread it as a concrete request and ask 'help with what?'; the correct response is simply 저도 잘 부탁드려요 — reciprocating the goodwill.

structuredNuance.t: 부탁 (付託) = 'entrusting a request' + 드려요 = humble 'I give you (upward)'. Literal: 'I humbly entrust a request to you.' Real meaning: 'please treat me/this kindly going forward' — a relationship-opening social pledge, not a specific task.

First meetings, joining a team, entrusting a task, saying goodbye after an arrangement. 부탁드려요 fits polite everyday settings; 부탁드립니다 or 부탁드리겠습니다 for formal business or very senior people. Never use casual 부탁해 upward — it can sound demanding.

도와주세요 = a concrete request for help with something specific. 잘 부탁드려요 = open-ended goodwill, no task implied. 도와주세요 cannot replace 잘 부탁드려요 at introductions, and 잘 부탁드려요 cannot replace 도와주세요 when you need actual assistance.
Scale up humility: 부탁해 → 부탁해요 → 부탁드려요 → 부탁드립니다 → 부탁드리겠습니다. Add scope with 앞으로 (going forward) or a noun: 이 일 잘 부탁드려요 (this task). The response is always 저도 잘 부탁드려요.

English speakers hear 'I ask a favor' and wait for the actual favor — there is none. It is pure social lubrication. Also, never mirror back with casual 부탁해 to a senior who just said 부탁드려요 — that drops a register and sounds presumptuous.

mistakes: Reading it as a concrete request and asking 'help with what?'
잘 부탁드려요 is a relationship phrase, not a task order; it asks for general goodwill, so just reply 네, 저도 잘 부탁드려요 rather than hunting for a chore.
Saying 부탁해 to a boss or someone older.
부탁해 is casual 반말; upward you need the humble 드리다 form 부탁드려요/부탁드립니다, or it sounds presumptuous.
Pairing it with 주세요 as 부탁드려 주세요.
부탁드리다 already contains the giving verb; stacking 주세요 is redundant. Use 부탁드려요 or 부탁드립니다 by itself.

examples: 바닥이 미끄러우니까 조심하세요!
The floor's slippery, so be careful!
Immediate safety warning; -으니까 = because — sets up the reason before the instruction.
A: 이제 갈게요. / B: 네, 밤늦었는데 조심히 들어가세요.
A: I'll head out now. / B: Sure, it's late — get home safe.
Classic parting exchange: A announces departure, B gives a caring farewell with 조심히 (adverb) + 들어가세요 (go inside/home).
요즘 독감이 유행이니까 감기 조심하세요.
The flu's going around these days, so take care not to catch a cold.
Health-worry variant: noun (감기) names the hazard before 조심하세요, showing the NOUN + 조심 pattern in a real sentence.
nuance: 조심하세요 is built on Sino-Korean 操心 'to manage/hold the heart-mind', literally 'keep your mind on guard', with 하세요 as the honorific imperative. It functions both as a live safety warning and as a caring farewell, the way English 'take care' covers both 'watch out right now' and 'look after yourself'. The key structural pattern is NOUN + 조심하세요, where the noun names the hazard: 발 조심 (step), 계단 조심 (stairs), 감기 조심 (cold), 차 조심 (cars) — the object particle 을/를 is normally dropped in these set phrases and sounds stiff if kept. The critical grammar split: 조심하다 (verb, 'be careful') and the adverb 조심히/조심해서 ('carefully') are different forms — 조심히 가세요 means 'go carefully', not 조심하세요 가세요. Compared to 조심하세요, 주의하세요 (from Sino-Korean 注意) is more formal and sign-like ('Caution!' on a placard), while 조심하세요 is warmer and conversational. Drop the 요 to 조심해 only with close friends or juniors.

structuredNuance.t: 操心(조심) = 'manage/guard the heart-mind' + 하세요 = honorific imperative. Literal: 'please hold your mind in check.' Real: 'be careful / take care' — used both as an in-the-moment safety warning and as a warm send-off.

Anyone to anyone in a polite relationship: strangers, shopkeepers, friends-of-friends, elders. 조심하세요 (존댓말) for most people; 조심해 (반말) only to close friends, children, or juniors. The NOUN + 조심하세요 pattern — 발 조심하세요, 감기 조심하세요 — is especially common for caring seasonal or daily-life warnings.

주의하세요 (注意) = formal, sign-like 'Caution' — seen on warning placards or official announcements. 조심하세요 = warmer, conversational, personal concern. As farewells: 잘 가세요 = 'go well (safe travels)'; 조심히 가세요 = 'go carefully', adding the nuance of personal vigilance.
Adverb variants: 조심히 + motion verb (조심히 가세요, 조심히 내려가세요). Noun hazard: 발/계단/차/감기 + 조심하세요. Stronger: 꼭 조심하세요 ('please be sure to be careful'). Softest casual: 조심해.

English speakers add the object particle in NOUN + 조심: 발을 조심하세요 — natural Korean drops it, just 발 조심하세요. Also, they try 조심하세요 가세요 to mean 'go carefully', but you need the adverb form: 조심히 가세요 or 조심해서 가세요.

mistakes: Using 조심하세요 to mean 'go carefully' before a verb of motion.
As a standalone it means 'be careful', but to modify 가다 you need the adverb form: 조심히 가세요 / 조심해서 가세요, not 조심하세요 가세요.
Forcing the object particle in NOUN+조심: 계단을 조심하세요.
Fixed warnings drop the particle: 계단 조심하세요, 발 조심하세요. Adding 을/를 sounds stiff and textbook-like.
Saying 조심해 to a stranger or elder.
조심해 is bare 반말 and can sound like an order; to anyone you don't know well use the honorific 조심하세요.

usage: 잘 makes it humbler, not 'know well'
examples: 글쎄요, 잘 모르겠어요.
Hmm, I'm really not sure.
글쎄요 is the standard hesitation cushion before admitting uncertainty — together with 잘 모르겠어요 it sounds humble, not evasive.
A: 이 서류 어떻게 작성해요? / B: 저도 잘 모르겠어요. 담당자한테 물어보세요.
A: How do I fill out this form? / B: I'm not sure either. Try asking the person in charge.
Workplace A/B: B's 저도 ('me too / I also') keeps the tone collaborative rather than dismissive; 담당자 = person in charge.
언제 끝날지 아직 모르겠어요.
I still don't know when it'll finish.
-ㄹ지 embeds the unknown future fact inside 모르겠어요, showing the EMBEDDED QUESTION structure essential for real speech.
nuance: 모르다 is the antonym of 알다 'to know', and the -겠- before the polite -어요 ending softens the assertion into 'I can't seem to tell / I'm not certain' rather than a blunt fact. This makes 모르겠어요 notably more humble and polite than 몰라요 — which, without -겠-, can sound curt or even dismissive, like 'I don't know and that's that'. Use 모르겠어요 with customers, teachers, seniors, or anyone you're being careful with; 몰라요 is fine between close friends. Adding 잘 (잘 모르겠어요) counterintuitively intensifies the not-knowing — it does NOT mean 'I know well'; in negative verbs, 잘 boosts the negative, meaning 'I really have no idea'. The -ㄴ지/-ㄹ지 construction embeds questions inside 모르겠어요: 어디인지 모르겠어요, 맞는지 모르겠어요, 언제 오실지 모르겠어요 — this pattern is essential for natural speech. Compare 안 알아요: Korean does not negate 알다 with 안; the dedicated negative is 모르다, making 안 알아요 wrong for 'I don't know'.

structuredNuance.t: 모르다 = 'to not know' + -겠- = epistemic softener + -어요 = polite ending. The -겠- is NOT future tense here; it hedges the claim. Literal: 'I (seemingly) don't know.' Real meaning: 'I'm not sure / I can't quite tell' — more tentative and humble than plain 몰라요.

모르겠어요 = polite, for service contexts, seniors, teachers, strangers. 모르겠습니다 = formal 합쇼체, office/official settings. 모르겠어 = casual, friends and peers. 몰라요 = neutral but blunter; fine between friends but can sound curt to superiors.

몰라요 = flat fact, can sound dismissive. 모르겠어요 = hedged, polite, open to reconsidering. 기억이 안 나요 = 'I can't recall' (memory issue, not ignorance). 잘 모르겠어요 = 'I really have no idea' (stronger negative, not 'I know well').
Embedded questions: [clause]-ㄴ지/-ㄹ지 + 모르겠어요 (어디인지, 언제 오실지, 맞는지). Add 아직 for 'not yet': 아직 모르겠어요. Strengthen with 정말: 정말 모르겠어요. Full formal: 모르겠습니다.

잘 모르겠어요 looks like 'I know (잘) well' — but 잘 before a negative verb intensifies the negative: it means 'I truly have no idea'. Also, never say 안 알아요 for 'I don't know': 알다 is negated only by the separate verb 모르다, not by 안 + 알다.

mistakes: Reading 잘 모르겠어요 as 'I know it well'.
잘 here intensifies the negative verb, so it means 'I really don't know', the opposite of what 잘 ('well') suggests in English.
Defaulting to 몰라요 with strangers or superiors.
몰라요 sounds blunt, even cold; the -겠- in 모르겠어요 adds politeness and humility, which is safer in service or formal settings.
Saying 안 알아요 for 'I don't know'.
Korean does not negate 알다 with 안; the dedicated antonym verb is 모르다. Use 몰라요 / 모르겠어요, never 안 알아요.

examples: 잠깐만요!
Hold on a sec!
Rapid stop-signal when someone is about to walk away or do something — the clipped form works as an interjectional grab of attention.
A: 이제 출발할까요? / B: 잠깐만요, 전화 좀 받을게요.
A: Shall we head off? / B: One second — let me grab this call.
-ㄹ게요 announces B's own next action; B is not asking permission, just signaling a tiny delay.
잠깐만요, 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me, let me get past.
Subway/crowd context: used exactly like English 'excuse me, coming through' — the wait-request doubles as an attention-getter for physical space.
nuance: 잠깐 means 'a brief moment', 만 is the limiter particle 'only/just', and 요 makes it polite — so 잠깐만요 is literally 'just a brief moment, please', covering both 'hold on a sec' (asking to wait) and 'excuse me' (getting attention or space), the way English 'one second' or 'excuse me' pulls double duty. The near-twin 잠시만요 uses 잠시, the more literary synonym for 'a moment'; 잠시만요 leans slightly more formal and is preferred in service announcements or with older strangers, while 잠깐만요 is everyday conversational. Neither is rude, but 잠깐만요 without the 요 — bare 잠깐만 — drops into 반말 and can sound abrupt to strangers. Compare with 기다려요 ('wait'), which is a direct command; 잠깐만요 is gentler because 만 limits the imposition to 'only a tiny moment'. The full 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 is grammatically complete but sounds over-elaborate in quick spoken exchanges where the clipped form is natural.

structuredNuance.t: 잠깐 = 'a brief moment' + 만 = limiter 'only/just' + 요 = politeness. Literal: 'only a brief moment, please.' Real uses: (1) 'hold on / wait a sec', (2) 'excuse me, coming through / may I have your attention' — same word, two jobs depending on whether you're asking for time or physical space.

잠깐만요 = polite everyday speech, anyone you're not on casual terms with. 잠시만요 = slightly more formal, service contexts, elders, announcements. 잠깐만 (no 요) = 반말, close friends or juniors only. Never bare 잠깐만 to strangers.

잠시만요 = same meaning, marginally more formal. 기다려요 = blunt command 'wait'; 잠깐만요 is gentler because it frames the request as tiny (만). 실례합니다 = formal 'excuse me' for interrupting someone; 잠깐만요 is faster and more casual for the same purpose.
Scale up to full request: 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 (please wait a moment). Expand with reason: 잠깐만요, 메모 좀 할게요 ('hold on, let me take a note'). Casual short: 잠깐만!
English speakers over-formalize: they say 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 for every situation, but fast Korean conversation just uses 잠깐만요. Separately, they drop 요 with strangers — bare 잠깐만 is 반말 and sounds abrupt.
chips: 잠깐만요 is the natural fast form

mistakes: Dropping the 요 with strangers: just 잠깐만.
잠깐만 alone is 반말 and can sound abrupt or even rude to someone you don't know; keep the polite 요 — 잠깐만요.
Confusing it with 잠깐 as a noun meaning 'briefly'.
잠깐 by itself is the adverb/noun 'for a moment' (그는 잠깐 왔어요); 잠깐만요 is the fixed interjection 'hold on'. They aren't interchangeable in a sentence.
Using 잠깐만요 to make someone wait a long time.
It promises only a tiny pause (만 = just); for a real wait, say 조금만 기다려 주세요 or give a time, or it feels misleading.

examples: 천만에요.
You're welcome.
Stock textbook reply right after 감사합니다 — correct and polite but noticeably formal in casual settings.
A: 도와주셔서 정말 감사해요! / B: 아이고, 천만에요. 별거 아닌데요.
A: Thank you so much for your help! / B: Oh, not at all — it was nothing, really.
B layers two deflectors: 천만에요 + 별거 아닌데요 ('it's no big thing') for warm, humble effect — natural adult speech.
감사합니다. — 천만의 말씀이에요.
Thank you. — Not at all (please don't say such things).
천만의 말씀이에요 is the full-sentence form; 말씀 (honorific 'words') adds deference and is suitable for formal or business settings.
nuance: 천만에요 comes from Sino-Korean 千萬 'ten million' + 에요, an idiom meaning 'not in ten million ways' — i.e. 'don't even think of it / not at all'. It is the dictionary-correct reply to 감사합니다, but modern everyday Korean more naturally deflects with 아니에요 ('no, no'), 뭘요 ('oh, it was nothing'), or 별말씀을요, so 천만에요 can sound formal or slightly old-fashioned to younger ears. The register ladder for answering thanks: casual 응/아냐 (반말, very close friends) → 아니에요 (warm, everyday) → 천만에요 (polite but stiff) → 천만의 말씀이에요 (most deferential). A crucial boundary: 천만에요 only answers thanks; 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you flatter me'), so they are not fully interchangeable. English speakers mapping 'you're welcome' one-to-one onto 천만에요 will use it in casual contexts where 아니에요 or 뭘요 fits far better. Keep the 요; bare 천만에 alone is very rarely said.

structuredNuance.t: 千萬(천만) = 'ten million' + 에요 = copula. Idiom meaning: 'not even in ten million ways would that be worth thanks' → 'don't mention it / you're welcome'. It is a frozen idiom — do not parse 천만 as an actual number.

천만에요 suits polite adult speech and formal occasions. In casual daily conversation, younger Koreans prefer 아니에요, 뭘요, or 에이, 별거 아니에요. Reserve 천만에요 for moments that warrant formality, or it sounds stiff.

아니에요 = warm everyday 'no, no it's fine'. 뭘요 = casual downplayer, very natural. 천만에요 = polite but dated-feeling. 별말씀을요 = deflects BOTH thanks AND compliments. The key line: 천만에요 answers thanks only; 별말씀을요 also handles 'you're so kind / talented'.
Full sentence: 천만의 말씀이에요 (most deferential, business/formal). Soften with a lead-in: 아이고, 천만에요. Cascade: 아니에요, 천만에요, 별거 아니에요. Casual: 뭘요 / 아냐 (반말).

English speakers treat 천만에요 as the go-to 'you're welcome' for all contexts, but it sounds textbook-stiff in everyday conversation. Also, it does not work after compliments — for that, use 별말씀을요, not 천만에요.

mistakes: Using 천만에요 constantly because it's the 'textbook' answer.
It sounds formal and a bit dated; natives more often say 아니에요 or 뭘요 in casual situations, so reserve 천만에요 for politer moments.
Treating 천만에요 and 별말씀을요 as identical.
천만에요 answers thanks only; 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you flatter me'). Swapping them in a compliment context feels off.
Parsing 천만 literally as 'ten million'.
Here it's a frozen idiom 千萬 meaning 'by no means / not at all'. Trying to translate the number word-for-word misses that it's a set expression.

usage: Humble reply to thanks or praise
examples: 별말씀을요.
Don't mention it.
Quiet, self-effacing deflection on its own — the shorter the reply, the more modestly humble it reads.
A: 덕분에 정말 잘 끝났어요! / B: 별말씀을요, 잘 하셨어요.
A: It went so well thanks to you! / B: Not at all — you did great yourself.
덕분에 = thanks to (you); B deflects AND redirects the credit — very natural polite exchange between adults.
정말 친절하시네요. — 별말씀을 다 하세요.
You're so kind. — Oh, you flatter me.
Here 별말씀을요 deflects a compliment, not thanks — the key use case that distinguishes it from 천만에요.
nuance: 별말씀을요 breaks into 별 (別 'special, out of the ordinary') + 말씀 (the humble/honorific word for 'someone's words') + 을 (object particle) + 요, literally 'such special words (you say)!' — a set idiom that humbly protests any praise or thanks directed at you. Its register is courteous and gently self-effacing, natural among adults in polite settings. The defining advantage over 천만에요 is scope: 천만에요 only answers 감사합니다, but 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you're amazing', 'you're so kind'), because you're waving off the 'special words' the other person offered. The fuller form 별말씀을 다 하세요 ('you say all sorts of wonderful things') is even more vigorous in brushing off praise. Pronunciation note: 을요 naturally links in speech as [으료], and 말씀 must stay honorific — substituting plain 말 gives 별말, which means 'a strange/odd remark', the opposite of the intended modesty. In very casual speech among close peers, 뭘요 or 아니야 replace 별말씀을요.

structuredNuance.t: 별 (別 = special/extraordinary) + 말씀 (honorific 'words') + 을 (object particle) + 요. Literal: 'such special words (you say)!' — protesting that the thanks or compliment is far more than you deserve. Real: 'don't mention it / you flatter me'.

Adults in polite everyday or semi-formal settings — deflecting thanks after helping someone, or deflecting compliments about your skills or character. Too formal for very close friends; among peers say 뭘요, 아니야. Works well in service, educational, and professional contexts.

천만에요 = deflects thanks only; stiff. 아니에요 = warm everyday 'no, no'. 별말씀을요 = deflects both thanks and compliments; polite and humble. 별말씀을 다 하세요 = stronger form, mainly for compliments ('you really flatter me').
더 강하게: 별말씀을 다 하세요. Double deflect: 아니에요, 별말씀을요. With reassurance: 별말씀을요, 당연히 해야 할 일이에요. Casual equivalent: 뭘요. 반말: 뭘, 아냐.

The common spelling error is 별말씀요 or 별말요 — the object particle 을 must stay: 별말씀을요. More importantly, replacing 말씀 with plain 말 changes the meaning entirely: 별말 = 'a strange remark', which is rude. Pronunciation: 을요 links to sound like [으료].

mistakes: Shortening it to 별말요 or 별말씀요 and dropping the object particle.
The set phrase keeps 말씀 plus 을: 별말씀을요. 별말 alone means 'an odd remark', which changes the meaning entirely.
Assuming it only answers thanks like 천만에요.
별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you flatter me'). Using it after praise is correct and natural, which 천만에요 can't always cover.
Using plain 말 instead of the honorific 말씀.
The humility of the phrase depends on 말씀, the respectful word for someone's speech; 별말 sounds wrong and even slightly negative.

usage: Get home safe and come again
examples: 안녕히 가세요! 또 오세요!
Goodbye! Come again!
Cheery shout as a customer leaves — staff may overlap both phrases for a warmer send-off.
A: 잘 먹었습니다. / B: 맛있게 드셨어요? 다음에 또 오세요.
A: That was a great meal. / B: Did you enjoy it? Please come again.
Classic restaurant farewell exchange: A's gratitude triggers B's invite — only the host staying behind issues the 오세요.
감사합니다! 다음에 또 오세요, 조심히 가세요.
Thank you! Please come again — take care going home.
Cashier layering both the come-back invite and a safe-home wish in one warm send-off.
nuance: 다음에 ('next time') + 또 ('again') + 오세요 (honorific imperative of 오다 'to come') = 'please come again next time' — the standard warm send-off from staff or hosts to departing guests. The direction of the verb is crucial: the host uses 오다 (come toward me) because from their perspective the customer returns toward them; 가다 (go away from me) would be a directional error. The word 또 ('again, also') does the 'come back' work; 다시 ('again, redo') sounds like you're asking for a repeat of something that went wrong, so 다시 오세요 can inadvertently imply the visit wasn't good enough. One-way flow: this is the host's line, not the guest's — a customer should not say 다음에 또 오세요 to the shop; instead, reply with 잘 먹었습니다 or 감사합니다. Casual short form: 또 오세요 alone is friendly and common; 다음에 또 오세요 adds the 'next time' warmth. Mutual farewell between friends uses 다음에 봐요 ('see you next time') or 다음에 또 봐 (반말), not 오세요.

structuredNuance.t: 다음에 = next time + 또 = again + 오세요 = honorific imperative of 오다 'to come'. Literal: 'please come again next time.' Real: the host's warm standing invitation to return — social glue that ends a commercial or hosting interaction on a warm note.

Said exclusively by the person staying (shop, restaurant, host) to the person leaving (customer, guest). Never said by the guest to the host. Register: 오세요 = polite standard; if the customer is a VIP senior, 또 방문해 주세요 ('please visit again') is even more formal. Casual short: 또 오세요.

다음에 봐요 = mutual casual farewell between equals ('see you next time'). 다음에 또 오세요 = host-to-guest, directional. 다시 오세요 = sounds like the visit needs to be redone (avoid). 또 오세요 = friendly shorter version of the same phrase.
Shorter: 또 오세요. Layered: 조심히 가시고 또 오세요. Formal: 다음에도 방문해 주세요. 반말 (to a young regular): 또 와요 / 또 와.

Guests sometimes mirror 다음에 또 오세요 back to the staff — this is the host's line only. Guests reply with 잘 먹었습니다 / 감사합니다. Second trap: 다시 오세요 feels like a logical 'come again' but implies a redo, not a warm repeat visit.

mistakes: Saying 다음에 또 가세요 to invite someone back.
From the host's view the customer comes toward them, so the verb is 오다 → 오세요. 가세요 ('go') reverses the direction and sounds wrong.
A customer repeating 또 오세요 to the staff.
This is the host's line; customers reply with 네, 감사합니다 or 잘 먹었습니다, not by inviting the staff to 'come again'.
Swapping 또 for 다시 as 다음에 다시 오세요.
다시 nudges toward 'redo/once more'; for 'come another time' natives say 또. 다시 오세요 can hint you did something wrong the first time.

usage: Here it is / here you go
examples: 여기 있어요.
Here you go.
Said while physically extending something — the action and the phrase happen simultaneously; no additional words needed.
A: 영수증 드려요? / B: 괜찮아요, 됐어요. 거스름돈 여기 있어요.
A: Would you like a receipt? / B: No thank you — here's your change.
Cashier exchange: B pairs 괜찮아요 ('it's fine/no need') with the handover phrase; 거스름돈 = change.
주문하신 아메리카노 여기 있어요.
Here's the Americano you ordered.
Server placing a drink: the item name precedes 여기 있어요, pinpointing which drink is being presented, common in cafes.
nuance: 여기 있어요 = 여기 ('here, this place') + 있어요, the polite form of 있다 'to exist / to be located' — literally 'it is here', used the moment you physically hand or present something, like English 'here you go / here it is'. 있다 is the existence-and-location verb (opposite of 없다); do not substitute 이다 'to be (identifying)', so 'here it is' is 여기 있어요, never 여기 이에요. A critical distinction: the clipped 여기요 is the standard call for a server in a restaurant ('excuse me, over here!') — the same root word but a completely different function, distinguished by whether you are holding something out (여기 있어요) or signaling for attention (여기요). The negative is 여기 없어요 ('it's not here'), using 없다, not 안 있어요. The formal version 여기 있습니다 is used in polished service settings. In fast daily exchange, Koreans may also just say 여기요 while extending an item to a familiar person, but this risks ambiguity with the server-call; adding 있어요 removes all ambiguity.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 = 'here (this place)' + 있어요 = polite 있다 'to exist/be located'. Literal: 'it exists here.' Real: 'here you go / here it is' — accompanies the physical act of handing something over. The existence verb 있다 points to the item's location, not its identity.

여기 있어요 = standard polite handover (service, shopping, daily life). 여기 있습니다 = formal service register, polished staff. Casual 여기 있어 = 반말 only, close friends. 여기요 = completely different function — calling a server.

여기요 = call for a server ('excuse me/over here'), NOT a handover phrase. 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you') = announces the giving action, while 여기 있어요 = presents the item as already in hand. 여기 있어요 is presentation; 드릴게요 is announcement.
Formal: 여기 있습니다. With item name: [거스름돈/영수증/주문하신 음식] + 여기 있어요. With invitation to take: 여기 있어요, 받으세요. Casual: 여기 있어 (반말).

English speakers use bare 여기요 trying to say 'here you go' when handing something — but 여기요 calls a server. Add 있어요 when presenting an item. Also, 여기 없어요 (not here) uses 없다, never 안 있어요 — 있다 negates only with its own antonym.

mistakes: Using bare 여기요 to mean 'here you go' when handing something over.
여기요 alone is the call for a server ('excuse me!'). To present an item, say the full 여기 있어요, or the listener hears 'waiter, over here'.
Saying 여기 이에요 instead of 여기 있어요.
Location/existence uses 있다 (있어요), not the identifying copula 이다 (이에요). 여기 이에요 is ungrammatical for 'it's here'.
Negating with 여기 안 있어요 for 'it's not here'.
있다 has its own antonym 없다; 'it's not here' is 여기 없어요, not 안 있어요.

usage: How much time does it take?
examples: 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요?
How long to the airport?
-까지 = up to/as far as, the standard particle for marking the destination endpoint of a journey duration question.
A: 지하철로 얼마나 걸려요? / B: 한 20분쯤 걸려요.
A: How long by subway? / B: About 20 minutes.
Natural travel exchange: -로 marks means of transport; 쯤 = roughly/about, essential for approximating.
택배로 보내면 얼마나 걸려요?
If I send it by courier, how long will it take?
-면 = if/when condition; -로 marks the delivery method — shows 걸려요 covering non-travel durations like shipping.
nuance: 얼마나 걸려요? = 얼마나 ('how much / to what degree') + 걸리다 'to take (time), to be required', polite form. The verb 걸리다 carries three unrelated senses: (1) to take time (시간이 걸리다), (2) to hang/be caught (그림이 걸리다, 범인이 걸리다), (3) to catch an illness (감기에 걸리다) — context always disambiguates. The critical distinction from 얼마예요? is the verb: 얼마예요 asks PRICE (using the copula 이에요), while 얼마나 걸려요 asks DURATION (using 걸리다); swapping them gives you a cost when you wanted a time, or vice versa. Sharpen the question with front-loaded modifiers: destination 까지 (집까지), means 로 (버스로, 걸어서), and start-point 에서/서 (여기서). 시간이 in front is optional — 걸리다 already implies time. Standard answer forms: 30분쯤 걸려요 (about 30 min), 한 시간 정도 걸려요 (about an hour), 별로 안 걸려요 (doesn't take long).

structuredNuance.t: 얼마나 = 'how much/how far' + 걸려요 = polite form of 걸리다 'to take (be required)'. Literal: 'how much does it require?' Real: 'how long does it take?' — a duration question, not a cost question.

Asking a stranger on the street, a hotel receptionist, a delivery service, a taxi driver — all polite everyday settings. 얼마나 걸려요? = standard polite. 걸려? = 반말 (close friend). Formal: 얼마나 걸립니까? or 소요 시간이 어떻게 됩니까? for business/official contexts.

얼마예요? = price question (copula 이에요). 얼마나 걸려요? = duration question (verb 걸리다). These are entirely different structures. Also: 걸리다 meaning 'to take time' vs 걸리다 meaning 'to catch (illness)' — 감기에 걸리다 is illness, 시간이 걸리다 is duration; don't confuse.
Add destination: [장소]-까지 얼마나 걸려요? Add means: 걸어서/버스로/지하철로 얼마나 걸려요? Add start: 여기서 얼마나 걸려요? Answers: 쯤/정도 for approximations. 별로 안 걸려요 = 'it doesn't take long'.

Mixing up 얼마예요? (price) and 얼마나 걸려요? (time). The extra syllable 나 and the verb 걸리다 are both signals of duration. Also: marking the destination with -에 (location marker) instead of -까지 (extent marker): for 'how long TO a place' use -까지.

mistakes: Asking 얼마예요? when you mean 'how long does it take?'
얼마예요? asks the price; duration needs the verb 걸리다 → 얼마나 걸려요? Mixing them gets you a cost, not a time.
Marking the destination with -에 instead of -까지.
For 'how long TO a place', the goal-of-extent particle is -까지: 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? -에 marks a static location, not the endpoint of travel time.
Saying 얼마나 시간 걸려요 with no particle on 시간.
If you state the time noun, mark it as subject: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? Or just drop 시간 entirely — 얼마나 걸려요? already means 'how long'.

examples: 이거 뭐예요?
What is this?
Bare pointing question — natural while holding or tapping an unfamiliar item; the whole meaning is in gesture + phrase.
A: 이거 뭐예요? 매워요? / B: 이건 떡볶이인데요, 좀 매워요.
A: What's this? Is it spicy? / B: This is tteokbokki — it's a bit spicy.
Food stall A/B: B uses 이건 (이것은, topic marker) to gently introduce the answer; 인데요 softens the information delivery.
이 버튼 뭐예요? 누르면 어떻게 돼요?
What's this button? What happens if I press it?
이 + noun directly (no 것/거), then a natural follow-up: -면 어떻게 돼요? = 'what happens if I…' — shows 이거 뭐예요 as an opener to a fuller inquiry.
nuance: 이거 뭐예요? = 이거 (casual contraction of 이것 'this thing') + 뭐 (colloquial contraction of 무엇 'what') + 예요 (polite copula) — the everyday 'what is this?' spoken while pointing. Three contraction layers are standard in speech: 이것 → 이거, 이것이 → 이게 (with subject particle), 무엇이에요 → 뭐예요. 이거 뭐예요? and 이게 뭐예요? mean the same thing; the latter adds the subject particle for a marginally more deliberate delivery. Distance vocabulary: 이거 (near speaker) / 그거 (near listener) / 저거 (far from both) — match the word to where the object actually is. A crucial social rule: 뭐 (what) is for THINGS; asking about PEOPLE with 뭐예요 ('what are you?') is rude and grammatically wrong — 누구예요? ('who is this/are you?') is required. For function rather than identity, add 뭐 하는 거예요? or 어디에 써요? ('what's it used for?'). The copula fuses: write 뭐예요, not 뭐 이에요.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 = this thing (spoken form of 이것) + 뭐 = what (spoken form of 무엇) + 예요 = polite copula. Literal: 'this thing — what is it?' Real: 'what is this?' — identity question about a nearby object, usually accompanied by pointing.

이거 뭐예요? = polite everyday speech, fine with shopkeepers, staff, strangers. 이게 뭐예요? = same meaning, slightly more careful pronunciation. 이거 뭐야? = casual 반말, close friends only. 이것이 무엇입니까? = very formal, almost written — not said in conversation.
이거 뭐예요? = what IS it (identity). 이거 뭐 하는 거예요? = what does it DO (function). 이게 누구 거예요? = whose IS it (ownership). For PEOPLE: never 뭐예요? — always 누구예요? or 이분이 누구세요?
Distance variants: 이거/그거/저거 + 뭐예요? With noun: 이 [음식/버튼/단어] 뭐예요? Follow-up question: 어디에 써요? / 어떻게 써요? Casual: 이거 뭐야?
Using 뭐예요? for a person ('what are you?') is rude and wrong — use 누구예요? or 이분 누구세요?. Also, writing or saying 뭐 이에요 as two words is unnatural — the copula fuses: 뭐예요, one unit.

mistakes: Using 이거 뭐예요? about a person.
뭐 (what) is for things only; asking 'who is this?' takes 누구 → 이분 누구세요? Using 뭐예요 for a person is grammatically wrong and sounds rude.
Writing 이것이에요 / 무엇이에요 in casual speech.
Spoken Korean contracts these to 이게 / 뭐예요. The full forms are correct but sound stiff and written; natives say 이거 뭐예요?
Mixing up the distance words 이거/그거/저거.
이거 = near me, 그거 = near you, 저거 = away from both. Pointing at a far object but saying 이거 confuses the listener about which thing you mean.

usage: Polite heads-up about your own move
examples: 잠깐 화장실 좀 다녀올게요.
I'll just pop to the restroom.
다녀오다 = go and come back — implies you'll return promptly; more complete than 쓸게요 alone and very natural before a meeting or meal.
A: 저기요, 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? / B: 네, 들어가세요.
A: Excuse me, may I use the restroom? / B: Sure, go right in.
Cafe/shop permission exchange: A uses the -아도 돼요? form to genuinely ask; B's 들어가세요 = 'please go in', confirming it's fine.
밥 먹기 전에 화장실 좀 쓸게요.
I'll just use the restroom before we eat.
-기 전에 = before doing [something]; the phrase signals a brief departure and implicit return, softened by 좀.
nuance: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 = 화장실 (化粧室, literally 'makeup/grooming room', the standard polite term for toilet/restroom) + 좀 (lubricating softener, worn-down 조금 'a little') + 쓸게요, the -ㄹ게요 form of 쓰다 'to use'. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the defining feature: it announces your own intention as a polite heads-up ('I'm going to do this — just letting you know'), not a request for permission. This contrasts sharply with -아도 돼요? 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? ('may I use the restroom?'), which genuinely asks permission. Use the -ㄹ게요 form at a friend's apartment or in a meeting room where it's obviously OK; use the -아도 돼요? form in a shop or someone's home where you are not certain. 좀 is purely a politeness softener here — 화장실 쓸게요 without it is grammatical but slightly blunt; 화장실 좀 쓸게요 is warmer. 화장실 is the standard neutral term; 변소 is crude and dated. A common natural alternative: 화장실 좀 다녀올게요 (using 다녀오다 'go and come back') emphasizes you'll return.

structuredNuance.t: 화장실(化粧室) = 'grooming room' (standard polite term for restroom) + 좀 = softener + 쓸게요 = -ㄹ게요 form of 쓰다 'use'. Literal: 'I intend to use the restroom (a little).' Real: polite self-announcement — 'just letting you know I'm stepping out to use the restroom', NOT a request for permission.

Announcement (화장실 좀 쓸게요 / 다녀올게요) = at a friend's home, office, classroom, any place where permission is assumed. Permission ask (화장실 좀 써도 돼요?) = at a shop, stranger's home, formal venue. Casual: 화장실 좀 쓸게 (반말, drop 요). Very formal: 화장실 좀 다녀오겠습니다.

화장실 좀 쓸게요 = announce intent, you expect it's fine. 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? = genuinely request permission. 화장실 좀 다녀올게요 = 'I'll pop to the restroom and be right back' (implies return). 화장실 어디예요? = asking location, not announcing or asking permission.
With return: 화장실 좀 다녀올게요. With timing: 밥 먹기 전에 / 시작 전에 화장실 좀 쓸게요. Formal: 잠시 화장실 다녀오겠습니다. 반말: 화장실 좀 쓸게 / 다녀올게.

Using the announcing -ㄹ게요 form when permission is actually needed — in a shop or stranger's home, switch to 써도 돼요?. Also, treating 좀 as a literal quantity ('use the restroom a little') — it is a social softener, not a measure.

mistakes: Using 쓸게요 when you actually need permission.
-ㄹ게요 announces your own plan, not a request. In someone's home or a shop, ask 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? with the permission ending -아도 돼요.
Treating 좀 as the literal 'a little'.
Here 좀 is a politeness softener that smooths the request, not a quantity. 화장실 좀 쓸게요 doesn't mean 'use the restroom a little'.
Calling the room 변소 or asking 화장실 있어요? to find it.
변소 is crude/dated; the neutral polite word is 화장실. To locate it, ask 화장실 어디예요?, not just 'is there a restroom?'
